# Animals and humans

Alternative splicing is near-universal in human genes, and that fact alone
settles very little. A gene can produce twenty transcripts without any of them
mattering, and a gene can produce two transcripts that do opposite things. The
cases in this chapter are the ones where the isoform difference has been tied to
a phenotype, because those are the cases that carry the argument.

## Dscam1: diversity by combination {#sec-dscam}

*Drosophila* *Dscam1* is the most extreme demonstration available that a single
gene can specify an enormous protein repertoire, and the most thoroughly
dissected example of what such a repertoire is for.

The architecture is combinatorial rather than additive. Three clusters of
mutually exclusive exons, holding 12, 48 and 33 variants, are spliced so that
exactly one variant from each cluster appears in a mature transcript. The
product of those three choices is 19,008 distinct ectodomains, and pairing each
with one of two alternative transmembrane exons gives the 38,016 figure usually
quoted [@dong2023dscamscreen].

![Three mutually exclusive exon clusters and one alternative transmembrane exon
generate the *Dscam1* repertoire. A single neuron uses a small, probabilistically
drawn slice of it.](../figures/dscam-combinatorics.svg){#fig-dscam width=100%}

The arithmetic is worth stating plainly because the number is often quoted as a
curiosity about splicing capacity. It is better understood as a specification. The
Dscam1 ectodomain binds homophilically with near-absolute specificity: each
isoform recognises itself and binds other isoforms weakly or not at all
[@dscam2004homophilicbinding]. An isoform is therefore usable as a cell-surface
identity label, and the size of the repertoire sets how many distinguishable
labels exist.

What a neuron does with that label is repulsion. Sister dendrites of one neuron
carry the same isoforms, so they recognise each other and turn away, while
branches of different neurons pass freely. The recognition happens in the
variable ectodomain, but the conversion into repulsion is carried out by the
cytoplasmic tail [@dscam2007dendriteselfavoidance]. Self-avoidance thus requires
only that a neuron's isoform set be distinctive, not that it be any particular
set, which is consistent with how little of the repertoire a single cell uses:
R3/R4 photoreceptors were estimated to express on the order of 14 to 50 distinct
isoform mRNAs each [@dscam2004stochasticbiased].

Mutual exclusivity is enforced in *cis*, by RNA structure rather than by a
trans-acting factor choosing among equals. A single intronic docking site pairs
with the selector sequence upstream of one variable exon at a time, physically
presenting that exon and no other to the upstream constitutive exon
[@dscam2005dockingselector].

### How much diversity is required

Two experiments separate correlation from requirement. Alleles cutting the
maximum repertoire from 38,016 to 22,176 still produced specific connectivity
defects in mechanosensory neurons, establishing that the number itself is under
selection [@dscam2006diversityrequired]. A later CRISPR deletion series spanning
396 to 18,612 possible ectodomains then showed that there is no single
requirement to measure. Dendrite self/non-self discrimination saturated at about
2,000 isoforms and was indifferent to which cluster supplied them. Normal axon
patterning needed many more and depended on which clusters were present
[@dong2023dscamscreen]. Diversity does two jobs with different currencies: one
needs a sufficient count, the other needs particular identities.

### Bias, and a tension in the standard model

Isoform usage is not uniform across the repertoire, and the skew is itself
functional. Flies with normal Dscam1 protein levels and an unchanged number of
possible isoforms, but a globally shifted exon 9 usage distribution, showed
marked mushroom-body defects; the equivalent shift at exon 4 did not
[@dscam2021splicingbias]. Changing bias damaged axonal wiring without affecting
the self-avoidance of axonal branches, which is the function the isoform count is
thought to underwrite [@dscam2021splicingbias].

That result sits awkwardly with the standard account, and the authors say so:
strong reproducible bias restricts access to the very diversity that
self-avoidance is supposed to exploit [@hong2019dscamsplicingbias]. The tension
is unresolved, and the chapter leaves it that way.

## Splicing as a developmental switch

*Dscam1* uses splicing to generate variety. The *Drosophila* somatic
sex-determination cascade uses it to make a decision, and it remains the
clearest case of a splicing switch controlling a developmental outcome.

The cascade is a chain of splice choices. Female Sex-lethal protein acts
directly on RNA, binding the *transformer* transcript at or near its
non-sex-specific 3' acceptor and forcing use of the downstream, female-productive
acceptor [@sxl1990trasplicesite]. At the bottom of the chain Tra and Tra2 act
positively, recruiting SR-family factors to a regulatory element downstream of
the female-specific 3' splice site of *doublesex*; that assembled complex commits
the pre-mRNA to the female pattern [@dsx1993spliceenhancercomplex].

*doublesex* is also the cleanest demonstration that two isoforms of one gene can
do opposite things. The female product represses male differentiation and the
male product represses female differentiation, both as functional products of the
same primary transcript [@dsx1989sexspecificpolypeptides].

## Isoform switching within a cell's lifetime

Developmental cascades set an isoform once. CD45 shows the same machinery used
reversibly, as part of ordinary immune function.

Human CD45 produces five transmembrane phosphatase isoforms differing only in
their extracellular domains, through inclusion or skipping of variable exons 4, 5
and 6. Resting peripheral T cells carry long forms retaining two or three of
those exons; activated T cells express forms lacking most or all of them
[@cd452005variableexonelements]. The ectodomain length is consequential rather
than cosmetic: in T cell lines carrying a defined receptor, the short exon-null
isoform characteristic of memory CD4 cells supported antigen recognition best
[@cd451994isoformsrecognition]. The splice choice tunes signalling sensitivity
without altering receptor specificity.

## Opposing functions from one gene

The *bcl-x* locus was described from the outset as producing two spliced products
that pull in opposite directions, with the short form acting against the
pro-survival activity of bcl-2 rather than merely failing to protect cells
[@bclx1993dominantregulator].

The structural basis is a single internal deletion. Bcl-xS lacks 63 amino acids
spanning the conserved BH1 and BH2 regions, the segment giving Bcl-xL its closest
similarity to Bcl-2. The mechanism is less settled than the antagonism. The
original characterisation found Bcl-xS binding Bcl-xL only weakly in vitro, saw
no observable heterodimers in cells, and argued on that basis that its mechanism
differs from other pro-apoptotic family members
[@bclx1996santagonizesl]. A later review states the mechanism as direct
inhibition, with Bcl-xS binding and inhibiting Bcl-xL and Bcl-2 and thereby
releasing Bak [@stevens2019bclxsplicing]. The antagonism is solid; the
heterodimer model rests on the review rather than on the primary report.

## Isoforms that set tissue mechanics

Titin is the extreme case of a spliced product whose physical properties are the
phenotype. The adult human heart expresses a long compliant N2BA form of roughly
3,200 to 3,500 kDa alongside a short stiff N2B form of about 3,000 kDa, both
spliced from one gene of 364 exons [@li2022rbm20titinstiffness]. The mechanical
difference traces to how much extensible material the transcript retains: the
compliant form keeps a larger share of PEVK and immunoglobulin-like spring
elements in the I-band.

One factor dominates the ratio. RBM20 is the principal regulator of titin
pre-mRNA, and losing one functional copy shifts splicing toward highly compliant
isoforms and impairs the Frank-Starling response [@li2022rbm20titinstiffness].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why a spliced-out segment changes stiffness

Titin spans half a sarcomere and behaves like a spring in series with the
contractile machinery. Its I-band region contains tandem immunoglobulin-like
domains that unfold under load and a PEVK segment that behaves as an entropic
spring. Retaining more of these elements in the mature transcript lengthens the
spring, so the same stretch produces less restoring force. Splicing is not
modulating an activity here; it is changing how much polymer sits between two
anchors.
:::

## Ligand specificity by mutually exclusive exon

In FGFR1 through FGFR3, the mutually exclusive IIIb and IIIc exons encode the
C-terminal half of immunoglobulin loop III, which sits in the ligand-binding
site. The splice choice changes which fibroblast growth factors the receptor can
respond to at all [@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing].

The two forms are not interchangeable in development. Deleting the IIIb exon in
mouse is lethal, while deleting IIIc instead produces skeletal malformations
[@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing]. Usage is partitioned by tissue compartment,
with IIIb in epithelia and IIIc in mesenchyme, and a IIIb-to-IIIc switch in an
epithelial tumour is associated with increased invasiveness in bladder and
prostate cancer [@holzmann2011fgfrigiiisplicing].

## A cautionary case: PKM1 and PKM2

Pyruvate kinase M is the standard illustration of how much can hang on a
mutually exclusive exon pair, and also an illustration of how a widely repeated
isoform story can outrun its evidence.

Antisense oligonucleotides blocking an enhancer in exon 10, forcing exon 9
inclusion, killed glioblastoma cells, with the death attributed specifically to
loss of PK-M2 rather than to gain of PK-M1 [@wang2012pkmantisense]. That the
splice choice is consequential when forced is well supported.

The usual framing goes further, holding that tumours switch from PKM1 to PKM2.
Absolute mass spectrometry across 25 human cancers with tissue-matched controls
found PKM2 predominant in tumours and equally predominant in the matched normal
tissue, leading those authors to reject a tumour-associated switch
[@bluemlein2011pkmnoshift]. The defensible statement is that forcing the choice
has a large phenotype, not that tumours make the switch.

## How much of this is functional

Three bodies of evidence bear on whether the bulk of alternative splicing
resembles the cases above, and they do not agree.

**Tissue regulation is extensive.** The 2008 tissue survey identified over 22,000
tissue-specific alternative transcript events and estimated, by extrapolating
from expression bins, that between 52 and 80 per cent of events of each type are
tissue-regulated [@wang2008alternative]. Exons switching most sharply between
tissues were also most likely to preserve reading frame in both isoforms, read by
those authors as evidence that switch-like splicing makes two intact proteins
rather than shutting a gene off [@wang2008alternative].

**Much of the catalogue is not conserved.** A human-mouse comparison predicted
only about 2,000 alternatively spliced exons conserved between the species, found
those to be markedly more frame-preserving and domain-sparing than other events,
and concluded that the great majority of alternative splicing in the human EST
record is not conserved in mouse [@conservedas2005humanmouseexons]. The same
split appears in invertebrates: in *C. elegans*, splicing events differing
between tissues are preferentially frame-preserving and better conserved across
*Caenorhabditis* species than other alternative exons [@koterniak2020celegansplicing].

**A substantial fraction is error, and another fraction is neither error nor
protein diversity.** De novo junction discovery found about 150,000 previously
unannotated junctions in human cells, with little evolutionary conservation at the
new splice sites and an implied error rate near 0.7 per cent per intron, lower in
highly expressed genes [@pickrell2010noisysplicing]. Separately, one transcript
usually dominates: roughly 85 per cent of protein-coding mRNA in primary tissues
came from each gene's major transcript, though about 35 per cent of genes switch
which transcript dominates between tissues, and those authors declined to
conclude that minor transcripts are functionless
[@gonzalezporta2013dominanttranscript].

A third position reframes the question. Measuring unproductive splicing across
eight assays gave threefold more of it than steady-state RNA had suggested, with
15 per cent of transcript molecules from protein-coding genes unproductive, and
trait-associated loci acting through splicing were as often explained by
decay-driven expression changes as by isoform usage
[@fair2024unproductivesplicing]. On that account much alternative splicing is
neither protein diversity nor noise, but a mechanism for controlling how much
protein a gene makes.

These results are compatible. Most splicing events are rare, unconserved and
probably inconsequential; a minority are switch-like, frame-preserving and
conserved; and a further portion regulates expression level through decay. The
cases earlier in this chapter are drawn from the second group, and nothing here
licenses treating every annotated isoform as a functional entity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What the "95 per cent" figure actually counts

Two 2008 papers put alternative splicing at roughly 95 per cent of human
multi-exon genes, and the number is now quoted without its conditions.

Extrapolating by read coverage gave about 98 per cent of multi-exon genes
excluding cell lines, and about 100 per cent using all samples. Requiring a minor
isoform to reach 15 per cent frequency in at least one sample dropped this to 92
per cent of multi-exon genes, or roughly 86 per cent of all human genes
[@wang2008alternative]. The independent survey reached about 95 per cent of
multi-exon genes by a different route, and put intermediate- to high-abundance
splicing events in major tissues at about 100,000 [@pan2008deepsurveying].

Three things vary between these statements: whether the denominator is multi-exon
genes or all genes, what abundance threshold a minor isoform must clear, and
whether detection is direct or extrapolated. Quoted without them, "95 per cent"
is not wrong so much as uninterpretable.
:::
